summary.text: Principal component analysis is a linear technique that transforms data so the directions capturing the largest variation can be easily identified.
The first principal component explains the most variance, and each next one explains the most of what is left once earlier ones are removed.
The components are eigenvectors of the data's covariance matrix, so they are computed by eigendecomposition or singular value decomposition.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Principal component analysis, or PCA, is a linear way of cutting down the number of dimensions in a data set. People use it to explore data, to draw it, and to prepare it for later work. PCA moves the data onto new coordinate axes, chosen so that the directions holding the most variation are easy to pick out. Those directions are called principal components.

paragraphs.heading: Ranking the components
paragraphs.text: The first principal component is a new variable made by mixing the original variables in a linear way, chosen to explain as much variance as possible. The second explains the most variance in what is left after the first has been taken out. Repeating this through all p variables eventually accounts for all of the variance. PCA is most often used when many variables are strongly correlated and you want a smaller, independent set in their place.

paragraphs.heading: Lines that fit best
paragraphs.text: Each component can also be seen as a line through the data. It is the line that fits the points best while staying at right angles to every earlier component. Here, best means that the squared perpendicular gaps between the points and the line are as small as possible on average. Equivalently, each component points in the direction that makes the variance of the projected data largest. In the basis the components form, the separate dimensions of the data are linearly uncorrelated.

paragraphs.heading: Where eigenvectors come in
paragraphs.text: Both views lead to the same answer: each principal component is an eigenvector of the covariance matrix of the data. In practice you first center each variable on zero by subtracting its mean from every value. You then compute the covariance matrix, find its eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and rescale each eigenvector to unit length. Dividing one eigenvector's eigenvalue by the sum of all the eigenvalues gives the share of the variance that direction carries. The components can also be found from the singular value decomposition of the data matrix.

paragraphs.heading: An ellipsoid around the data
paragraphs.text: A helpful image is a p-dimensional ellipsoid fitted to the data. Each axis of that ellipsoid is one principal component. If an axis is short, the data vary only a little along it.

paragraphs.heading: PCA at work
paragraphs.text: Many studies plot data using only the first two principal components, which puts it in two dimensions where clusters of closely related points can be seen. PCA is used in population genetics, in microbiome studies and in atmospheric science, among other fields. Scree plots, which show how much variance is explained, and biplots help people read the results.

paragraphs.heading: Where it came from
paragraphs.text: Karl Pearson invented PCA in 1901, modelling it on the principal axis theorem of mechanics. In the 1930s Harold Hotelling developed it again on his own and gave it its name. Among the true multivariate analyses built on eigenvectors, it is the simplest, and it is closely tied to factor analysis.
